etymology: Hebrew Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh (H1961 + H834 + H1961) — "I will be what I will be" or "I AM that I AM"; God's self-revelation of His name to Moses at the burning bush (Exod 3:14), the source of the Tetragrammaton YHWH (Yahweh), and the name Christ explicitly applied to Himself in John 8:58.
biblical_def: I AM That I AM is the most theologically dense name of God in Scripture — the self-existing, self-defining, time-transcending Name God revealed to Moses at the burning bush. When Moses asked God what to tell the Israelites when they ask for His name, God answered: "I AM THAT I AM... Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you" (Exod 3:14). The Hebrew Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh is built on the verb "to be" (hayah) — God names Himself by being itself, the only entity that is its own ground of existence. From this self-revelation comes YHWH (Yahweh / Jehovah), the tetragrammaton, the personal covenant name of God. The supreme weight of this name appears in John 8:58 when Christ Himself claimed it directly: "Before Abraham was, I AM." The Greek egō eimi — without a predicate — is the Septuagint's translation of Ehyeh; Christ's listeners understood instantly what He was claiming and "took they up stones to cast at him" for blasphemy. Christ also uses egō eimi in His seven Johannine "I AM" sayings (bread of life, light of the world, door, good shepherd, resurrection and the life, way truth life, true vine) — each applying the divine Name to His own person and work. To confess Jesus is Lord is to confess Him as the I AM of the burning bush — eternal, self-existing, God Himself.
webster_summary: God's self-revelation of His Name to Moses at the burning bush; the source of YHWH; the Name Christ explicitly applied to Himself (John 8:58).
webster_full: I AM THAT I AM, noun. The Name by which God revealed Himself to Moses at the burning bush (Exod 3:14). Hebrew Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh. The source of the tetragrammaton YHWH (Yahweh).
Christ applied this Name to Himself: "Before Abraham was, I AM" (John 8:58). His listeners understood and took up stones to kill Him for blasphemy.
scriptures: Exodus 3:14
And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am. Then took they up stones to cast at him: but Jesus hid himself, and went out of the temple.
John 18:5-6
They answered him, Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus saith unto them, I am he. And as soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground.
Revelation 1:8
I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty.
corruption_summary: I AM is corrupted when modernist scholarship reduces the burning-bush revelation to evolved Yahweh-worship rather than direct divine self-disclosure, or when Christ's John 8:58 claim is downgraded to mere prophetic self-importance rather than the explicit divine self-identification His hearers correctly perceived.
corruption_paragraphs: Evolutionary-religion reduction. Source-critical Old Testament scholarship often treats the Exodus 3:14 revelation as the product of evolved Israelite religion — a god-name developed over centuries rather than directly revealed at the burning bush. But the canonical text presents it as direct revelation in a specific moment, and the NT (Christ Himself) treats it as such. To strip the direct-revelation event is to lose the gospel logic: the same God who revealed Himself to Moses now reveals Himself in the Son who applies the same Name to His own Person.

John 8:58 dismissal. Modern liberal theology often softens Christ's "Before Abraham was, I AM" to merely "I existed before Abraham" — a striking but not divine claim. But the Greek egō eimi without a predicate is the LXX translation of Exodus 3:14; Christ's hearers immediately understood the divine claim and tried to stone Him for it (John 8:59). The grammar, the response of the audience, and the canonical context all confirm: Christ claimed to be the I AM of Exodus 3:14. To soften this is to deny what the text plainly says and what the original audience plainly heard.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh (H1961 + H834 + H1961) — "I will be what I will be"; God's self-revealed Name; the source of YHWH.

Source of the tetragrammaton YHWH (Yahweh) — the personal covenant Name of God in the OT
Greek egō eimi (without predicate) — Septuagint translation; the formula Christ uses in John 8:58 and the seven Johannine I AM sayings
Self-existence, time-transcendence, ground-of-being-itself — the only Name where God names Himself by being itself
usage: I AM THAT I AM — God's self-revelation at the burning bush; the only Name where God names Himself by being itself.
Before Abraham was, I AM — Christ's direct claim to be the same I AM Moses met at the burning bush.
When the soldiers came to arrest Christ in Gethsemane and He said "I am he," they went backward and fell to the ground — the divine Name has weight.

etymology: Hebrew Shaddai (H7706) often combined with El (God) to form El Shaddai; Greek Pantokratōr (G3841) — "All-Ruling"; the Name of God emphasizing His omnipotent sovereignty, frequent in Job and in Revelation.
biblical_def: The Almighty is one of God's great Names — the Name of His OMNIPOTENT SOVEREIGNTY over all that exists. The Hebrew El Shaddai appears 48 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in patriarchal narrative (Gen 17:1; 28:3; 35:11; 48:3) and in Job (31 times — the book where God's sovereignty is most relentlessly defended). The Greek Pantokratōr ("All-Ruling") translates Shaddai in the LXX and dominates the Book of Revelation, appearing 9 times in Revelation alone (1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 15:3; 16:7, 14; 19:6, 15; 21:22). "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty" (Rev 1:8) — the climactic divine self-identification of the entire canon, applied to Christ. The four living creatures around the throne sing "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty" (Rev 4:8) — eternal worship of the All-Ruling One. The Name carries a specific theological weight: it is the Name God reveals when He calls Abraham to walk before Him and be perfect (Gen 17:1), when He blesses Jacob (Gen 35:11), and when His people need assurance that NO force can thwart His covenant. The Almighty cannot be overruled, outflanked, surprised, or defeated. Every promise He makes is backed by omnipotence. Every threat He utters is enforceable. The Christian's confidence rests not on his own strength but on the Name of the One whose strength is by definition exhaustless.
webster_summary: God's Name emphasizing His omnipotent sovereignty; Hebrew El Shaddai, Greek Pantokratōr; the All-Ruling One who cannot be overruled.
webster_full: THE ALMIGHTY, noun. A Name of God emphasizing His omnipotent sovereignty. Hebrew El Shaddai ("God Almighty"), Greek Pantokratōr ("All-Ruling").
Frequent in patriarchal narrative (Gen 17:1; 28:3; 35:11; 48:3) and in Job (31 times); dominates Revelation (9 times — Rev 1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 15:3; 16:7, 14; 19:6, 15; 21:22).
scriptures: Revelation 1:8
I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty.
Genesis 17:1
And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, the LORD appeared to Abram, and said unto him, I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect.
Revelation 4:8

And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come.
Job 11:7
Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?
corruption_summary: The Almighty is corrupted when modernist theology shrinks God's sovereignty (open theism, process theology, neo-classical limited-God systems), or when prosperity theology turns omnipotence into a wealth-distribution machine rather than the ground of covenant assurance.
corruption_paragraphs: Sovereignty-shrinking theologies. Open theism, process theology, and various "limited God" systems all soften the Almighty's omnipotence — God doesn't know the future, God grows along with creation, God's power is bounded by libertarian human will, etc. Each system makes God less than the canonical Almighty. The biblical Pantokrator is ALL-RULING — He doesn't share rule, doesn't grow, doesn't get surprised. Christian assurance rests on this; if God can be thwarted, no promise of His is secure. Modern attempts to make God more "relatable" by shrinking Him actually destroy the gospel's confidence.

Prosperity-distortion. The prosperity gospel often invokes the Almighty as a power-source for personal wealth — "the Almighty God will bless you with abundance." But canonical use of the Name is in covenant contexts ("walk before me and be thou perfect," Gen 17:1) and worship contexts (Rev 4:8). The Almighty is invoked as the ground of God's covenant fidelity and as the object of unceasing worship — not as a wealth-machine. Strip the Name of its covenantal and doxological context and you have made an idol of power-as-personal-resource.

Modern attempts to shrink God's omnipotence to make Him "relatable" actually destroy the gospel's confidence.

etymology: Hebrew Elyon (H5945), often El Elyon — "God Most High"; Greek Hupsistos (G5310). The Name of God's supreme exaltedness above all rivals, first used by Melchizedek in Genesis 14:18-20.
biblical_def: Most High is one of God's great titles emphasizing His SUPREME EXALTEDNESS above every rival deity, power, or authority. The Name first appears in Genesis 14:18-20 when MELCHIZEDEK, king of Salem and priest of El Elyon (God Most High), blesses Abraham after his victory over the four kings. Abraham accepts the blessing and tithes to Melchizedek, signaling that Abraham worships the same Most High God Melchizedek serves — the FIRST canonical glimpse that the Most High has worshippers outside the line of Abraham. The Most High recurs throughout Scripture: in the Psalms (the songs of Israel are full of Elyon language, especially Pss 91, 92, 107); in Daniel (the title used by the Babylonian Nebuchadnezzar after his madness — "I blessed the Most High," Dan 4:34); in the announcement of Christ to Mary ("He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest," Luke 1:32); and in demonic recognition (the Gerasene demoniac: "Jesus, thou Son of the Most High God," Mark 5:7). Note that pagan demons KNOW the title and use it accurately. The Most High is the God whose name acknowledges no rival — the title literally says "There is none higher." The pagans, the demons, the patriarchs, the Davidic psalmists, and the Christian fathers (Hebrews 7 expounds Melchizedek typologically of Christ) all converge on the same Most High God. To confess this Name is to deny every rival claim of divinity — the supreme exaltedness has no equal.
webster_summary: God's Name of supreme exaltedness above all rivals; Hebrew El Elyon; first used by Melchizedek; applied to Christ as Son of the Highest.
webster_full: MOST HIGH, noun. A Name of God emphasizing His supreme exaltedness above all rivals. Hebrew Elyon (H5945), often combined as El Elyon ("God Most High"). Greek Hupsistos (G5310).

First used by Melchizedek (Gen 14:18-20). Frequent in Psalms (especially Pss 91, 92, 107), Daniel, and the Lucan birth narratives ("Son of the Highest," Luke 1:32). Used by demons in recognition of Christ (Mark 5:7).
scriptures: Genesis 14:18-20

And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God. And he blessed him, and said, Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth: And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all.
Luke 1:32
He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David.
Mark 5:7
And cried with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not.
Psalm 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
corruption_summary: Most High is corrupted when interfaith universalism uses the title to suggest all religions worship the same God (Melchizedek's Most High and Abraham's God are the same; modern Allah and Christian Trinity are NOT), or when the title is reduced to vague generic deism.
corruption_paragraphs: Interfaith universalism. Some interfaith dialogue uses Melchizedek (the priest of God Most High outside Abraham's line) to argue that all religions essentially worship the same God under different names. But the canonical text is specific: Melchizedek worshipped the Most High God WHO IS the God of Abraham (the names line up exactly); his priesthood is later applied typologically to CHRIST (Heb 7), not to any non-Christian religion. The Most High has worshippers outside Israel's covenantal line (Melchizedek, Job, Naaman) — but they worship the SAME GOD who is later revealed as the Triune Yahweh in Christ. Modern Allah, Hindu deities, or vague generic deity-categories are not the canonical Most High.

Deistic flattening. Modern progressive theology sometimes treats "the Most High" as a generic supreme-being concept compatible with deism — God as exalted concept rather than personal covenant Lord. But the canonical Most High BLESSES Abraham, GIVES the throne of David to Christ, and is RECOGNIZED by demons as a specific, personal, judging Lord. The title is not abstract; it is the Name of a specific Person whose supreme exaltedness is over a specific creation and toward whom specific responsibility is owed.

etymology: Hebrew Qedosh Yisrael (H6918 + H3478) — the unique title of God overwhelmingly favored by the prophet Isaiah (25 of its 30+ OT occurrences are in Isaiah); combines holiness (the radical otherness of God) with covenantal particularity (the God OF Israel).
biblical_def: Holy One of Israel is the signature title of God in the book of Isaiah — appearing 25 times in Isaiah alone (more than in all the rest of the OT combined) and just a handful of times elsewhere (2 Kings 19:22; Pss 71:22; 78:41; 89:18; Jer 50:29; 51:5). The title combines two ideas that the prophets hold together: God's RADICAL OTHERNESS (holiness — separateness, transcendence, moral purity) and His COVENANTAL PARTICULARITY (the God OF Israel — specifically committed to this people, not deity-in-general). Isaiah's prophetic ministry was launched by his vision of the Lord in the temple (Isa 6) where the seraphim cry "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts" — three-fold holiness, the most intense form of emphasis in Hebrew. From that vision Isaiah carried forward the title that summed up what he had seen: the Holy One who is OF Israel, holy AND committed. The title appears in promises ("Thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel," Isa 41:14; 43:14; 47:4; 48:17; 49:7; 54:5; 55:5; 60:9, 14), in warnings ("They have despised the Holy One of Israel," Isa 1:4; 5:24; 30:11-12, 15), and in exaltations ("thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel," Isa 54:5). The dual-edged use is canonical: the Holy One of Israel is both the GROUND of Israel's hope and the WARNING to Israel's sin. Christ Himself — who is the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah's servant songs (Isa 42, 49, 50, 52-53) — is identified by Peter at Pentecost as "the Holy One" and "the Just" (Acts 3:14). The Holy One of Israel becomes flesh as the Holy One of God.
webster_summary: The signature title of God in Isaiah, combining radical holiness with covenantal commitment to Israel; applied to Christ as "the Holy One."
webster_full: HOLY ONE OF ISRAEL, noun. A Name of God combining His radical holiness (transcendent otherness, moral purity) with His covenantal particularity (commitment to Israel specifically). Hebrew Qedosh Yisrael.

Overwhelmingly favored by Isaiah (25 occurrences in Isaiah, compared to ~5 in the rest of the OT). Originates in Isaiah's temple vision (Isa 6) where the seraphim cry "Holy, holy, holy." Christ identified as "the Holy One" (Acts 3:14; cf. Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34).
scriptures: Isaiah 6:3
And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
Isaiah 41:14
Fear not, thou worm Jacob, and ye men of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.
Isaiah 54:5
For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called.
Acts 3:14
But ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you.
corruption_summary: Holy One of Israel is corrupted when the radical otherness is softened to "God is loving" without the awe of holiness, or when the covenantal particularity (the God OF Israel specifically) is dissolved into modernist universalism that loses the gospel's particularity (salvation is from the Jews, John 4:22).
corruption_paragraphs: Holiness-softening. Modern theology often emphasizes God's love at the expense of His holiness — "God is love" is true (1 John 4:8) but it is HALF of what 1 John 4 says (4:8 + the entire flow of the letter on righteousness, judgment, and propitiation). The Holy One of Israel is the God WHO IS LOVE AND WHO IS HOLY together — not love at the expense of holiness, not holiness at the expense of love. Isaiah's title preserves both: the Holy One who is THE REDEEMER (love made concrete in covenant rescue). Strip holiness and the love becomes sentimental; strip love and holiness becomes terror. Hold both.

Particularity-dissolution. Modern interfaith and progressive theology often dissolves the "of Israel" particularity — God is the God of all peoples equally, no special covenant with anyone. But the canonical title is specific: the God of ABRAHAM, ISAAC, AND JACOB; the God who chose ISRAEL out of all nations (Deut 7:6-8); the God whose Messiah comes from ISRAEL'S line and offers salvation "to the Jew first, and also to the Greek" (Rom 1:16). The gospel has a particular shape — universal in offer (all are invited), particular in origin (salvation is from the Jews, John 4:22). To dissolve the particularity is to make the gospel a generic spirituality.

Appears 25 times in Isaiah (more than in all the rest of the OT combined) — Isaiah's signature title
Christ identified as "the Holy One" by Peter (Acts 3:14); by demons (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34); by John (1 John 2:20)
usage: Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts — the seraphim's three-fold cry at Isaiah's commissioning gave him his lifelong title for God.
Thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel — the Reformed gospel held together: holiness AND redemption in the same Name.
Christ is the Holy One of Israel become flesh — the radically other God committed to His covenant people, now indwelling them.

etymology: Hebrew Adonei ha-Adonim (Deut 10:17), Greek kyrios kyriōn (G2962) — Lord of all lords, the supreme Lord above every other lord. Coupled with "King of Kings" in Rev 17:14 and 19:16 as the climactic title of the conquering Christ.
biblical_def: Lord of Lords is the title of God's supreme lordship over every other lord, king, ruler, or authority. The OT background is Deuteronomy 10:17 — "For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible." The title proclaims that whatever lords or rulers exist in heaven or earth, Yahweh is their Lord. In the NT, the title bookends Revelation as Christ's climactic identification: "the Lamb shall overcome them: for he is Lord of lords, and King of kings" (Rev 17:14) and on His vesture at the Second Coming: "And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS" (Rev 19:16). Paul also applies it: "the King of kings, and Lord of lords" (1 Tim 6:15). The title carries political weight in a Roman imperial context where Caesar claimed the title kyrios ("Lord"). For Christians to confess Jesus as Lord of Lords was a direct confrontation of imperial Caesar-worship: there is one Lord above every Caesar, and His name is Jesus. The title also has eschatological weight: it identifies Christ as the One who will personally judge every earthly authority. Every senator, every president, every king, every magistrate is responsible to this Lord — there is no lord whose authority Christ does not finally exceed and judge. To confess Christ as Lord of Lords is to deny every absolute claim of human authority.
webster_summary: The supreme Lord above every other lord; God's title of absolute lordship over all rulers; Christ's climactic title at His return (Rev 19:16).
webster_full: LORD OF LORDS, noun. A title of God emphasizing supreme lordship over every other lord, king, ruler, or authority. Hebrew Adonei ha-Adonim, Greek kyrios kyriōn.
OT background: Deut 10:17. NT climactic application: Rev 17:14; 19:16; 1 Tim 6:15 — applied to Christ as the conquering King-Lord above every earthly authority.
scriptures: Revelation 19:16
And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.
Deuteronomy 10:17
For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward.
Revelation 17:14
These shall make war with the Lamb, and the Lamb shall overcome them: for he is Lord of lords, and King of kings: and they that are with him are called, and chosen, and faithful.
1 Timothy 6:15
Which in his times he shall shew, who is the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords.
corruption_summary: Lord of Lords is corrupted when its political weight is privatized (made about personal devotion only, not about Christ's lordship over public authorities), or when it is reduced to vague theistic affirmation rather than the specific confrontation of every rival lordship.
corruption_paragraphs: Privatized-lordship reading. Modern evangelicalism often reduces "Jesus is Lord" to a private, personal-devotion category — Jesus is MY Lord, my heart-confession, but not the Lord above presidents, kings, magistrates, or cultural authorities. But the canonical title "Lord of LORDS" specifically asserts Christ's supremacy over OTHER LORDS — political, ecclesiastical, cultural. The early church understood this; when they confessed Jesus as Lord, they were denying Caesar's lordship at the cost of their lives. To make Christ's lordship privately devotional rather than publicly cosmic is to gut the title.

Theistic-vague reduction. Generic civil religion often invokes "the Lord" as a vague theistic affirmation without specifying which Lord. But the canonical title is sharp: Jesus is Lord of Lords; there is no other Lord whose lordship is not under His. Allah is not Lord of Lords; modern secular authority is not Lord of Lords; cultural consensus is not Lord of Lords. To confess Christ as Lord of Lords is to deny every rival claim. Vague theism cannot carry the canonical weight.

Every earthly authority is under the Lord of Lords; no Caesar, no president, no magistrate exceeds His authority.

etymology: Greek phōs tou kosmou (G5457 + G2889) — Light of the world; one of Christ's seven "I AM" sayings in John (John 8:12; 9:5; 12:46), echoing Isaiah 49:6 (the Servant as "a light to the Gentiles") and Isaiah 60:1-3 ("the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee").
biblical_def: Light of the world is one of Christ's seven great "I AM" sayings in John, by which He applies the divine Name to Himself: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life" (John 8:12). The saying came at the Feast of Tabernacles, when the temple court was lit by enormous lampstands commemorating the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness. Christ stood up at the climax of the feast and declared Himself the substance of what the lamps signified. The title has rich OT background: "The LORD is my light and my salvation" (Ps 27:1); the Servant of the LORD is given "for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth" (Isa 49:6); "Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee...And the Gentiles shall come to thy light" (Isa 60:1, 3). Christ takes all these threads and applies them to Himself: He is the light promised to lead the wilderness, the light to the Gentiles, the light that the redeemed will walk by in the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:23 — "the Lamb is the light thereof"). And He says to His disciples: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid" (Matt 5:14). Christ as primary Light makes His people derivative lights — moons reflecting the sun. The light of the world is not Christ AND His church together; it is Christ Himself, who shines AS the light AND shines THROUGH the church.
webster_summary: Christ's I AM saying applying the divine Name to Himself; the light that ends darkness for those who follow Him; ultimately the lamp of the New Jerusalem.
webster_full: LIGHT OF THE WORLD, noun. One of Christ's seven "I AM" sayings in John: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life" (John 8:12; cf. 9:5; 12:46).

Background: Isaiah 49:6 (Servant as light to the Gentiles); Isaiah 60:1-3 (the glory of the LORD risen upon Zion). Eschatological fulfillment: "the Lamb is the light thereof" of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:23).
scriptures: John 8:12
Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
John 9:5
As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.
Matthew 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Revelation 21:23
And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.
corruption_summary: Light of the world is corrupted when modern syncretism applies the title to any religious teacher (Buddha, Muhammad, Krishna all called "light"), or when the church appropriates the title in a way that displaces Christ as primary Light rather than derivative.
corruption_paragraphs: Syncretistic title-borrowing. Various religious traditions describe their founders as "light" — Buddha as the "enlightened one," Muhammad as a guide of light, Krishna as cosmic light, etc. Interfaith dialogue sometimes treats these as parallel claims, each true within its tradition. But Christ's claim is exclusive: "I am THE light of the world" — not one light among many. The seven I AM sayings are deliberate echoes of God's I AM name (Exod 3:14); Christ is claiming divine identity, not religious teacher status. No other "light" claim has the canonical weight to compete with this one.

Church-displaces-Christ. Matt 5:14 — "Ye are the light of the world" — is sometimes taken to mean the church is THE light, replacing Christ. But the canonical relationship is clear: Christ is PRIMARY light (John 8:12, etc.); the church is DERIVATIVE light, moons reflecting the sun (Matt 5:14-16 — "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and GLORIFY YOUR FATHER WHICH IS IN HEAVEN"). The church's light points beyond itself to the Father; if the church becomes its own end (institutional self-promotion, ecclesial pride), it has stopped being light and started being eclipse.
roots_summary: Greek phōs tou kosmou (G5457 + G2889) — light of the world; Christ's I AM saying applying the divine Name to Himself.
roots_lines: Greek phōs (G5457) — light; kosmos (G2889) — world; together: "light of the world"
One of Christ's seven Johannine I AM sayings: bread (6:35), light (8:12), door (10:9), good shepherd (10:11), resurrection (11:25), way (14:6), vine (15:1)
OT background: Ps 27:1; Isa 49:6 (Servant as light to Gentiles); Isa 60:1-3 (glory of LORD risen on Zion)
Eschatological fulfillment: "the Lamb is the light thereof" of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:23) — light needs no sun or moon
usage: I am the light of the world — Christ's I AM saying applying the divine Name to Himself at the Feast of Tabernacles.
Ye are the light of the world — the church is derivative light, moons reflecting the Sun who is Christ.
In the New Jerusalem there is no need of sun or moon — the Lamb is the light thereof.

etymology: Greek hē anastasis kai hē zōē (G386 + G2222) — "the resurrection and the life"; Christ's fifth I AM saying in John, spoken to Martha before raising Lazarus (John 11:25).
biblical_def: Resurrection and the Life is Christ's fifth I AM saying, spoken to Martha just before He raised Lazarus from the dead (John 11:25): "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?" The saying is structured in two halves, addressing two categories of believers. (1) "He that believeth in me, THOUGH HE WERE DEAD, yet shall he live" — those who die before Christ's return shall be raised from the dead at His coming (the resurrection of the body, 1 Cor 15). (2) "Whosoever LIVETH AND BELIEVETH in me shall never die" — those alive at Christ's return shall never see death (1 Thess 4:17 — caught up to meet the Lord in the air). Christ then asks Martha point-blank: "BELIEVEST THOU THIS?" — making the application personal: this is not abstract eschatology; it is a question of trust in Christ's specific person and word. Martha confesses: "Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world." Christ then proceeds to demonstrate the title concretely by calling Lazarus out of the tomb. The pattern is the gospel in miniature: Christ DECLARES the divine title; ASKS for faith from the believer; DEMONSTRATES the truth of the title in resurrection power. Christ does not just promise resurrection at the last day; He IS the resurrection — the personal source and ground of all resurrection life. Believers do not just receive resurrection FROM Him; they receive resurrection IN Him.
webster_summary: Christ's fifth I AM saying, spoken to Martha before raising Lazarus; Christ is not just the giver of resurrection life but the personal source and ground.
webster_full: RESURRECTION AND THE LIFE, noun. Christ's fifth "I AM" saying in John, spoken to Martha at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:25). "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die."
Two halves of the promise: dead-believers will be raised; living-believers will never die (cf. 1 Cor 15:51-54; 1 Thess 4:13-17).
scriptures: Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?

And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.
1 Corinthians 15:21-22
For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.

Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live. For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself.
corruption_summary: Resurrection and the Life is corrupted when modernist theology spiritualizes the resurrection ("He rose in our hearts" / "Christ lives on in his followers") rather than affirming the bodily resurrection Christ explicitly promises, or when the personal-faith demand ("Believest thou this?") is replaced with universal default-saving.
corruption_paragraphs: Spiritualized-resurrection theology. Modernist liberal theology often reduces Christ's resurrection to symbolic affirmation — He rose in the disciples' hearts, His teaching lives on, his spirit endures. But Christ's I AM saying is concrete: he RAISED LAZARUS bodily from the tomb to demonstrate the title. The resurrection is bodily, public, demonstrable. The same Christ who raised Lazarus will raise His people bodily at His return (1 Cor 15). To spiritualize resurrection is to deny the canonical demonstration and to empty the title "Resurrection and the Life" of its meaning.

Default-universalism replacing personal faith. "Believest thou this?" is the personal application Christ explicitly demanded of Martha. The promise of resurrection-life is conditional: "He that BELIEVETH in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Modern universalist theology often softens this — perhaps everyone will eventually be saved regardless of present faith. But Christ's question is sharp: do YOU believe? The title is a personal call to trust, not an automatic universal benefit.
roots_summary: Greek hē anastasis kai hē zōē (G386 + G2222) — the resurrection and the life; Christ's fifth I AM saying, at Lazarus's tomb.
roots_lines: Greek anastasis (G386) — resurrection; from ana (up) + histēmi (to stand)
Greek zōē (G2222) — life; the higher-quality life-as-such, often distinguished from bios (mere biological life)
Christ's fifth Johannine I AM saying (John 11:25), spoken to Martha at Lazarus's tomb before raising him
Two-fold promise: dead-believers raised at the last day; living-believers never die at the Second Coming
usage: I am the resurrection, and the life — Christ at Lazarus's tomb claimed the divine Name and then demonstrated it.
Believest thou this? — Christ's personal demand of Martha; not abstract eschatology but a question of trust.
Christ does not just GIVE resurrection life; He IS resurrection life; we receive it not FROM Him alone but IN Him.

etymology: Greek hē thyra tōn probatōn (G2374 + G4263) — "the door of the sheep"; Christ's third I AM saying in John (John 10:7, 9), part of the Good Shepherd discourse.
biblical_def: Door of the Sheep is Christ's third I AM saying, embedded in the Good Shepherd discourse of John 10. Christ uses it twice in quick succession: "I am the door of the sheep" (John 10:7) and "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture" (John 10:9). The image draws from ancient Palestinian sheepfold architecture. A sheepfold had a low stone wall around an open courtyard with a single opening — no actual hinged door. At night the shepherd himself slept across the opening, BECOMING the door with his body. Anyone wanting to harm the sheep had to go through the shepherd. Christ identifies Himself as this living door: He is the only legitimate entry point to the sheep, the protective boundary at night, and the gateway by which the sheep go OUT to pasture in the morning. The threefold promise is sweeping: "he shall be SAVED, and shall GO IN AND OUT, and FIND PASTURE." The door image carries exclusive force — there is ONE door, not many; "all that ever came before me are thieves and robbers" (John 10:8); "if any man enter in," not many doors but the single Christ-door. This connects with John 14:6 ("I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me") — the exclusive-mediator claim of Christ that the canonical text repeats in multiple metaphors (door, way, mediator, name under heaven by which we must be saved, Acts 4:12). The door image is also pastoral: Christ is not just the way in but the protective boundary that keeps wolves out and the leading-out for daily pasture.
webster_summary: Christ's third I AM saying; the only legitimate entry-point to the sheepfold of God's people, the protective boundary at night, and the gateway out to daily pasture.
webster_full: DOOR OF THE SHEEP, noun. Christ's third "I AM" saying in John (10:7, 9): "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved."
Image from ancient Palestinian sheepfold architecture — the shepherd slept across the single opening, becoming the door with his body. Carries exclusive force: ONE door, not many.
scriptures: John 10:7
Then said Jesus unto them again, Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep.
John 10:9
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
John 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Acts 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: Door of the Sheep is corrupted when modern inclusivism or pluralism dilutes the exclusive-mediator force ("many doors to God") or when the image is reduced to mere institutional church membership (the door becoming Romanism's sacramental system or evangelicalism's altar call).
corruption_paragraphs: Many-doors inclusivism. Modern interfaith dialogue often softens Christ's exclusive door-saying — "Christ is one door, but other religions have their own doors to God." But the canonical text is unambiguous: "I am THE door" (definite article); "by me if any man enter in"; "there is none other name under heaven" (Acts 4:12); "no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:6). The exclusive force is not a misreading; it is the explicit claim. To make Christianity one religion among many is to deny what Christ specifically said about Himself.

Institutional-door reduction. Some traditions effectively replace Christ as door with their institutional gatekeeping — the Roman sacramental system (no salvation outside the Roman Catholic Church), or hyper-evangelical altar-call mechanics (no salvation without praying the specific prayer). But Christ is the door, not the institution that points to Him. Any system that puts itself in the door-position blocks rather than opens the way to Christ. The door is Christ Himself; the church's only proper function is to point through Christ to the Father, never to substitute its own gate for His.
roots_summary: Greek hē thyra tōn probatōn (G2374 + G4263) — the door of the sheep; Christ's third I AM saying.
roots_lines: Greek thyra (G2374) — door, gateway, entrance
Greek probaton (G4263) — sheep; the people of God in the Good Shepherd discourse
Ancient Palestinian sheepfold architecture: open courtyard with a single opening; the shepherd slept across it, becoming the door himself
Threefold promise: SAVED (eternal life), GO IN AND OUT (daily access), FIND PASTURE (ongoing provision)
usage: I am the door of the sheep — Christ is the only legitimate entry to the fold of God's people.
By me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture — the threefold promise of the door.
The shepherd became the door by sleeping across the opening; Christ became our door by laying down His body in death.
related: The Way, the Truth, and the Life

etymology: Hebrew Tsemach Yahweh (H6780) — "Branch of Yahweh"; a Messianic title appearing principally in Isa 4:2; Jer 23:5; 33:15; Zech 3:8; 6:12 — the promised Davidic king who would be both shoot from a stump and the great priest-king ruling forever.
biblical_def: Branch of the LORD is one of the great Messianic titles of the OT, gathering up the prophetic expectation of a Davidic descendant who would unite kingly and priestly office and rule forever. The title appears at five major prophetic locations, each adding a facet: (1) ISAIAH 4:2 — "In that day shall the branch of the LORD be beautiful and glorious" (the Branch as the glory revealed in the day of the LORD); (2) ISAIAH 11:1 — though the word is netser (a related term), "there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots" (the Branch as shoot from the cut-down Davidic line); (3) JEREMIAH 23:5 — "I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth" (the Branch as righteous reigning king); (4) ZECHARIAH 3:8 — "behold, I will bring forth my servant the BRANCH" (the Branch as God's appointed servant); (5) ZECHARIAH 6:12-13 — "Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH... he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be A PRIEST upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both" (the Branch as priest-king uniting both offices that the OT had carefully kept separate, since Aaron's line and David's line were distinct). Christ fulfills all five: He is the glory revealed (Isa 4:2 / John 1:14), the shoot from Jesse's stump after the Davidic line had been cut down by the exile (Isa 11:1 / Matt 1), the righteous reigning king (Jer 23:5 / Rev 19), the Servant (Zech 3:8 / Phil 2:6-11), and the priest-king after the order of Melchizedek (Zech 6:12-13 / Heb 7). The Branch grows quietly from the stump no one expected to sprout.
webster_summary: A Messianic title gathering five prophetic locations (Isa 4:2; Isa 11:1; Jer 23:5; Zech 3:8; Zech 6:12); the Davidic shoot uniting kingly and priestly offices.
webster_full: BRANCH OF THE LORD, noun. A Messianic title appearing at five major prophetic locations: Isa 4:2; Isa 11:1 (related word netser); Jer 23:5; Zech 3:8; Zech 6:12-13. Hebrew Tsemach Yahweh.

The Branch is the promised Davidic descendant — shoot from a stump, righteous reigning king, God's Servant, and (uniquely) priest-king uniting offices that the OT had kept separate. All five fulfilled in Christ.
scriptures: Zechariah 6:12-13

Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD: Even he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.
Jeremiah 23:5
Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.
Isaiah 4:2
In that day shall the branch of the LORD be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent and comely for them that are escaped of Israel.
Isaiah 11:1
And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots.
corruption_summary: Branch of the LORD is corrupted when the priest-king typology of Zechariah 6:12-13 is severed from Christ's high-priestly work (Hebrews 7), or when each individual Branch passage is read in isolation rather than as a unified canonical chorus.
corruption_paragraphs: Priest-king severance. Zechariah 6:12-13 uniquely promises a Branch who would be BOTH king AND priest — "he shall be a priest upon his throne." The OT had kept these offices strictly separated: Aaron's line was priestly; David's line was royal; King Uzziah was struck with leprosy for trying to combine them (2 Chr 26:16-21). The Branch unites what the OT had carefully kept apart. Hebrews 7 expounds this: Christ as priest after the order of Melchizedek (not Aaron) holds both offices forever, fulfilling Zechariah 6:12-13 exactly. To strip this typology is to lose the key explanation of why Christ's priesthood is superior to Aaron's.

Isolated-passage reading. Modern preaching sometimes treats each Branch passage in isolation — Isaiah's Branch is one thing, Jeremiah's another, Zechariah's another. But the canonical pattern is unified: five passages, all using the same root tsemach (or related netser), all describing the same coming Messianic figure with complementary facets. The Branch is glory revealed (Isa 4:2), shoot from cut-down stump (Isa 11:1), righteous king (Jer 23:5), Servant (Zech 3:8), priest-king (Zech 6:12-13). To read them as five separate prophecies of five different things is to miss the Spirit's unified canonical work.

roots_lines: Hebrew tsemach (H6780) — branch, shoot, sprout; the Messianic title used by Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Zechariah
Related: Hebrew netser (Isa 11:1) — shoot, branch — different word but same Messianic concept; root of "Nazareth" / "Nazarene"
Five major Branch passages: Isa 4:2; Isa 11:1; Jer 23:5; Zech 3:8; Zech 6:12-13 — each adds a facet of the same coming Messiah
Unites kingly and priestly offices the OT had kept strictly separate — fulfilled in Christ as priest after Melchizedek (Heb 7)
usage: Behold the man whose name is the Branch — Zechariah's word for the Messiah who would be both king AND priest.
The Branch grows from the cut-down stump no one expected to sprout — Israel's Davidic line, dead in exile, sprouted in Bethlehem.
Christ fulfills all five Branch passages: glory revealed, shoot from Jesse, righteous king, Servant, priest-king after Melchizedek.

etymology: Hebrew Ebed Yahweh (H5650 + H3068) — "Servant of Yahweh"; the central figure of Isaiah's four "Servant Songs" (Isa 42:1-9; 49:1-13; 50:4-11; 52:13-53:12), the suffering Messiah who would bear the sins of many.
biblical_def: Servant of the LORD is the central title of the four "Servant Songs" of Isaiah — Isa 42:1-9; 49:1-13; 50:4-11; and the climactic 52:13-53:12 — which together prophesy a coming Servant who would unite suffering, intercession, and exaltation in a way no OT figure ever had. The four songs progressively reveal: (1) the Servant's QUIET MINISTRY — "He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street" (Isa 42:2), the gentle non-coercive proclamation; (2) the Servant's COMMISSION TO ISRAEL AND THE GENTILES — "It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob...I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth" (Isa 49:6); (3) the Servant's OBEDIENCE UNDER SUFFERING — "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting" (Isa 50:6); and most weighty, (4) the SUBSTITUTIONARY ATONEMENT — "He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:5). Isaiah 53 is the great prophetic chapter of substitutionary atonement, quoted by Christ Himself ("he was reckoned among the transgressors," Luke 22:37) and applied to Christ by the early church (Acts 8:32-35 — Philip and the Ethiopian eunuch; 1 Pet 2:21-25). The title "Servant" is also Christ's self-designation: "the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). The greatest title in the universe (Lord) is held by the One who took the lowest position (Servant) — and through Servant-obedience He was exalted to the highest Name (Phil 2:5-11).
webster_summary: The central figure of Isaiah's four Servant Songs; the suffering Messiah who bears the sins of many; the title Christ applied to His own ministry.
webster_full: SERVANT OF THE LORD, noun. The central figure of Isaiah's four Servant Songs: Isa 42:1-9; 49:1-13; 50:4-11; 52:13-53:12. Hebrew Ebed Yahweh.
Climactic in Isaiah 53 — the great prophetic chapter of substitutionary atonement ("He was wounded for our transgressions"). Fulfilled in Christ (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Pet 2:21-25; Mark 10:45).
scriptures: Isaiah 53:4-5

Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Isaiah 49:6

And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
Mark 10:45
For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
Philippians 2:7-9

But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him.
corruption_summary: Servant of the LORD is corrupted when Isaiah 53 is reduced to mere prophetic poetry about Israel's national suffering (collective-Israel-as-servant reading), or when the substitutionary-atonement doctrine of "bruised for our iniquities" is softened into example-only theology (Christ shows us how to suffer, but doesn't substitute for us).
corruption_paragraphs: Collective-Israel reading. Modern Jewish (and some modernist Christian) interpretation reads the Servant of Isaiah 53 as Israel collectively — the suffering nation as the Servant who bears the world's pains. But the New Testament treats it as INDIVIDUAL Messianic prophecy: the Ethiopian eunuch reads Isa 53 and asks Philip "of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man?" Philip's answer (Acts 8:35): he "preached unto him Jesus." Peter quotes Isa 53 about Christ's atonement (1 Pet 2:24-25). The canonical interpretation is individual-Messianic; collective-Israel readings are post-NT attempts to deflect the messianic claim.

Example-only atonement. Liberal theology often reduces "he was wounded for our transgressions" to Christ-as-moral-example: he showed us how to suffer nobly. But Isaiah 53 is explicit about substitution: "the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all" (53:6); "by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities" (53:11); "he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many" (53:12). The pile-up of substitutionary language is unmistakable: he TOOK what was OURS. Example theology removes the gospel by leaving us still bearing our own sin.

Four Servant Songs of Isaiah: 42:1-9 (quiet ministry); 49:1-13 (light to Gentiles); 50:4-11 (obedient suffering); 52:13-53:12 (substitutionary atonement)
Isaiah 53 is the great OT prophecy of substitutionary atonement — quoted by Christ (Luke 22:37) and the early church (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Pet 2:21-25)

usage: He was wounded for our transgressions — Isaiah's great prophecy of substitutionary atonement fulfilled in the Servant Christ.
The greatest Lord became the lowest Servant and was exalted to the highest Name — the gospel pattern of Phil 2:5-11.
Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth — the Father's word over the Son who would suffer for many.
